title: Red Wine Headache: Why It Happens and How to Stop It
excerpt: Why a glass or two of red wine can trigger a headache within the hour: the 2023 UC Davis quercetin finding, histamine and tannins, why sulfites are probably innocent, and how to get rid of a wine headache.
metaDescription: Why red wine gives you a headache within the hour: the UC Davis quercetin finding, histamine, tannins, the sulfite myth, and how to get rid of it fast.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The short answer:** if a glass or two of red wine gives you a headache within an hour or so, and the same amount of vodka or white wine doesn't, you're not imagining it. The most interesting recent explanation comes from a 2023 University of California, Davis lab study, which found that a compound in red grape skins called **quercetin** can be turned by your body into a form that blocks an enzyme your liver uses to clear a toxic by-product of alcohol. Histamine and tannins may also play a part for some people. Sulfites, the usual suspect, are probably not the cause for most people. None of these explanations is proven yet, and different people likely react to different things.

This page is about the headache that shows up **while you're drinking or soon after**, sometimes after just one glass. That's a different problem from the pounding head you wake up with the next morning. If that's what you're dealing with, our [wine hangover guide](/never-hungover/wine-hangover-guide) covers the morning-after side, and our broader [alcohol headache guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-headache-why-it-happens-how-to-prevent-2025) explains both types for all drinks.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article summarizes published research for general education. It doesn't replace a doctor who knows your health history. **Get urgent medical care** if a headache comes on suddenly and severely (the worst headache of your life, peaking within a minute), or comes with a stiff neck, fever, confusion, weakness or numbness on one side, slurred speech, vision loss, or fainting. Also talk to a doctor if wine reliably triggers migraines, if you get hives, wheezing, or swelling after drinking, or if your headaches are getting more frequent. In an emergency, call 911.

## Two Different Headaches: The "Wine Headache" vs. the Hangover

Headache specialists actually separate these. The International Classification of Headache Disorders (ICHD-3), the reference system doctors use to diagnose headaches, lists two kinds of alcohol-induced headache:

- **Immediate alcohol-induced headache** (sometimes called a "cocktail headache"). It starts within about three hours of drinking and fades within about three days, usually much sooner. In susceptible people it can follow a small amount of alcohol.
- **Delayed alcohol-induced headache**, which is the hangover headache. It shows up the next morning as your blood alcohol level falls back to zero, often after heavier drinking.

The red wine headache that people complain about, the one that hits halfway through the second glass, fits the first category. That matters because the causes and the fixes are different. A hangover headache is tied to how much you drank, poor sleep, dehydration, and inflammation. An immediate red wine headache can follow a small amount, which points toward something in the wine itself or how your body handles it, not simply the dose of alcohol.

| | Immediate red wine headache | Hangover headache |
|---|---|---|
| When it starts | Within minutes to about 3 hours | The next morning |
| How much wine | Can follow a single glass | Usually after several drinks |
| Likely drivers | Wine compounds (quercetin, histamine, tannins), alcohol widening blood vessels, migraine sensitivity | Total alcohol, poor sleep, dehydration, inflammation, acetaldehyde |
| Who gets it | A subset of people, often with migraine history | Almost anyone who drinks enough |
| Best first move | Stop drinking, water, food | Rest, fluids, food, a pain reliever if safe for you |

For the morning-after version, see our [hangover headache relief guide](/never-hungover/hangover-headache-fast-relief-methods-2025).

## The UC Davis Quercetin Finding (2023)

In late 2023, a team at UC Davis led by wine chemist Andrew Waterhouse, with Apramita Devi and headache researcher Morris Levin of UC San Francisco, published a study in *Scientific Reports* proposing a new explanation for red wine headaches. It got a lot of press, so it's worth being clear about what they actually found.

### How alcohol is normally cleared

To follow their idea, you need the two-step way your body breaks down alcohol:

1. An enzyme called alcohol dehydrogenase turns alcohol into **acetaldehyde**, a toxic chemical that causes flushing, nausea, and headache.
2. A second enzyme, **ALDH2** (aldehyde dehydrogenase 2), quickly turns acetaldehyde into harmless acetate.

Normally step two keeps pace with step one, so acetaldehyde never builds up much. When ALDH2 doesn't work well, acetaldehyde accumulates and people feel awful fast. That's exactly what happens in people with a common genetic variant of ALDH2, mostly of East Asian ancestry, who flush red and get headaches and a racing heart after small amounts of alcohol. (Our [Asian flush guide](/never-hungover/complete-guide-asian-flush-comprehensive) explains that in detail.) The drug disulfiram, used to discourage drinking, works on the same principle: it blocks this enzyme so that drinking makes people sick.

### What the researchers found

The UC Davis team screened a set of compounds found in red wine to see which could block ALDH2. Quercetin stood out. Quercetin is a flavonoid (a type of plant pigment) that grapes make to protect themselves from sunlight, and it's concentrated in grape skins. Red wine is fermented with the skins, so it carries much more quercetin than white wine.

When you drink quercetin, your body converts much of it into a form called **quercetin glucuronide**. In lab tests, that converted form inhibited ALDH2. The researchers' hypothesis: drinking red wine delivers both alcohol and quercetin, the quercetin glucuronide slows down ALDH2, acetaldehyde builds up, and in susceptible people that triggers a headache, along with flushing and other symptoms, within a short time.

### Why this explanation is appealing

- It explains why **red wine** is worse than white wine or spirits at the same alcohol dose. The difference is the skins.
- It explains why the headache can follow **just one or two glasses**, unlike a hangover.
- It would explain why some people react and others don't, if people differ in how much quercetin they absorb and convert, or in how much ALDH2 activity they have to spare.
- It fits with the observation that **some red wines bother people and others don't.** Quercetin levels vary a lot from wine to wine. Grapes grown with their clusters exposed to more sun make more of it, and winemaking choices such as how long the juice sits on the skins also change the final amount.

### What it does not prove

This was a **lab study**, measuring enzyme activity in test tubes. It did not show that drinking red wine raises acetaldehyde enough to cause headaches in real people. The authors themselves described it as a hypothesis and said a human trial was the next step, comparing red wines with high and low quercetin. Until that kind of study is published and repeated, quercetin is a promising lead, not a settled answer.

It's also likely that red wine headaches have more than one cause. Quercetin may explain some people's headaches and not others. Keep that in mind as we look at the other suspects.

**A side note on quercetin supplements:** some people take quercetin capsules for allergies. Based on this research, it's at least plausible that taking a quercetin supplement around the time you drink could make an alcohol headache worse, though no one has tested this directly. If you take quercetin and notice headaches with alcohol, that's worth mentioning to your doctor.

## Histamine: Real Mechanism, Mixed Evidence

Histamine is the chemical behind many allergy symptoms, and it also widens blood vessels, which can trigger headaches. Fermented foods and drinks contain histamine, and red wine generally contains more than white wine.

Your gut normally breaks down histamine from food using an enzyme called diamine oxidase (DAO). Alcohol is thought to interfere with that enzyme, so drinking wine may give you a dose of histamine and reduce your ability to clear it at the same time. People with low DAO activity, a condition often called histamine intolerance, may be especially sensitive. They tend to react to other high-histamine foods too, like aged cheese, cured meats, and sauerkraut.

The trouble is that controlled studies haven't backed this up well. A double-blind study by Kanny and colleagues, published in the *Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology* in 2001, gave people who reported wine intolerance wines with low and high histamine content and found no clear link between histamine level and their reactions. Other researchers, notably Wantke and colleagues in Austria in the 1990s, reported that some patients with wine intolerance improved on a low-histamine diet. So the honest summary is that histamine may matter for a minority of people, especially those with broader histamine intolerance, but it doesn't look like the main explanation for most red wine headaches.

**What this means for you:** if you also get headaches, flushing, a stuffy nose, or itching after aged cheese, cured meats, or other fermented foods, histamine is a reasonable suspect, and it's worth talking to a doctor or allergist. Some people try a non-drowsy antihistamine before drinking; check with a pharmacist first, because some antihistamines cause drowsiness that alcohol makes worse.

## Tannins and Migraine

Tannins are the compounds that make red wine feel dry and grippy in your mouth. They come from grape skins, seeds, and stems, and from oak barrels. Red wine has far more than white.

The strongest evidence that something in red wine, not just alcohol, triggers headaches comes from migraine research. In a well-known study published in *The Lancet* in 1988, Littlewood and colleagues gave people who said red wine triggered their migraines either red wine or vodka mixed to the same alcohol content and disguised so they couldn't tell which was which. A good share of the red wine group developed migraines; none of the vodka group did. That points to a component of red wine as the trigger in those people.

Researchers have suggested tannins (or related phenolic compounds) as a candidate, partly because they can cause the release of serotonin, a brain chemical involved in migraine. That link is a theory rather than something proven in people. Tannins are found in tea and dark chocolate too, and those don't bother most wine-sensitive people, so they're probably not the whole story.

Surveys of people with migraine consistently list alcohol as a common trigger, with red wine reported more often than other drinks. A 2019 survey of Dutch migraine patients by Onderwater and colleagues, published in the *European Journal of Neurology*, found red wine was the drink people most often named as a trigger. Interestingly, many people with migraine in those surveys simply avoid alcohol, so the true picture may be even stronger than self-reports suggest.

**If you have migraines,** a headache after one glass of red wine may be a migraine attack triggered by the wine, not a separate "wine headache." That's worth knowing, because migraine has its own effective treatments that a doctor can prescribe.

## Myth Check: Are Sulfites Causing Your Wine Headache?

This is the most common explanation people give, mostly because US wine bottles carry a "Contains Sulfites" warning. The evidence doesn't support it for most people.

**What sulfites are:** sulfur dioxide and related compounds are used in winemaking to prevent spoilage and oxidation. Yeast also produce small amounts naturally during fermentation, so essentially all wine contains some, even wines labeled "no added sulfites." In the US, any wine containing more than 10 parts per million must carry the warning label.

**Why sulfites probably aren't the problem:**

- **White wine usually has more sulfites than red.** Winemakers often add more to white and sweet wines because they have fewer natural preservatives (red wine's tannins help protect it). If sulfites caused wine headaches, white wine should be worse, but people overwhelmingly blame red.
- **Many foods contain far more.** Dried fruit such as dried apricots, along with some packaged foods, can contain many times the sulfites of a glass of wine. People who get headaches from red wine usually don't get them from a handful of dried apricots.
- **The documented sulfite reaction isn't a headache.** True sulfite sensitivity is uncommon and mostly affects people with asthma. Its typical symptoms are wheezing, chest tightness, and sometimes hives, not a delayed headache.

So the label is real and sulfites matter a lot for that small group of sensitive people, usually with asthma. If you get breathing symptoms after wine, take that seriously and see a doctor. But for a plain headache after red wine, sulfites are an unlikely explanation, and "sulfite-free" wines aren't likely to solve it. Some people do report doing better on these wines, which may come down to other differences in how they're made.

## Other Things That Can Make It Worse

Alongside the wine-specific suspects, some general factors stack up:

- **Alcohol itself widens blood vessels.** Ethanol is a vasodilator, meaning it relaxes blood vessels, which can trigger headaches in people prone to them regardless of the drink. Red wine is also often drunk at a higher alcohol content than people assume, with many bottles at 14% or more.
- **Drinking on an empty stomach.** Alcohol hits your bloodstream faster when you haven't eaten, so acetaldehyde and any wine-specific compounds arrive faster too.
- **Drinking fast.** Pace matters for the same reason.
- **Dehydration and existing triggers.** Being short on sleep, stressed, or skipping meals lowers your headache threshold. A glass of wine can be the last straw on a day you were already close.
- **Other congeners.** Wine contains many by-products of fermentation besides the ones above. Researchers call these "congeners," and darker drinks generally contain more of them. Their role is clearer for hangovers than for immediate headaches. We cover them in our guide to [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol).

## How to Get Rid of a Wine Headache

If a headache is starting while you're drinking or shortly after, these steps are sensible and low-risk.

### 1. Stop drinking

This sounds obvious, but it's the most effective move. If the quercetin theory is right, more red wine means more of both the enzyme-blocker and the alcohol it's slowing down. If you want to keep drinking, switching to water is the best choice. Switching to a clear spirit or white wine is a distant second.

### 2. Drink water and eat something

A glass or two of water won't cure the headache on its own, but it helps if you're also a bit dehydrated. Food, especially something with carbohydrates and protein, slows alcohol absorption and can take the edge off.

### 3. Rest somewhere quiet and dim

If the headache has a migraine feel (throbbing, sensitivity to light or sound, nausea), lying down in a dark, quiet room is often the most helpful thing you can do. A cool cloth on the forehead or back of the neck helps some people.

### 4. Think carefully about pain relievers

This is where you need to be careful, because every common painkiller has a downside with alcohol:

- **Acetaminophen (Tylenol):** processed by the liver alongside alcohol. A single standard dose after a modest amount of wine is unlikely to harm a healthy person, but it's not something to take repeatedly while drinking, and it's riskier for regular heavy drinkers. See our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) for the details.
- **Ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin (NSAIDs):** easier on the liver but harder on the stomach. Alcohol already irritates the stomach lining, and the US label for these drugs warns about stomach bleeding for people who have three or more drinks a day. If you use one, take it with food and stick to the label dose. Our [Aleve and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/aleve-and-alcohol) explains the risks of naproxen specifically.

If you have a prescription migraine medication, ask your doctor whether it's safe to take after drinking, since the answer differs from drug to drug. Don't mix pain relievers, and don't take more than the label allows.

### 5. Skip the "hair of the dog"

More alcohol only delays the problem. It won't fix an acetaldehyde or vasodilation headache.

### 6. Know when it isn't a wine headache

A headache that is sudden and explosive, comes with a stiff neck, fever, confusion, weakness, or changes in vision or speech, or simply feels different from any headache you've had before, needs urgent medical attention whether or not you've been drinking. Don't assume it's the wine.

## How to Prevent Red Wine Headaches

If you'd like to keep drinking red wine without the headache, there's no guaranteed method, but these approaches are reasonable and you can test them on yourself.

**Keep the amount small and slow.** Since the immediate headache can follow a single glass, the dose that bothers you may be lower than you think. Try one glass with food, sipped over an hour, and see how you feel.

**Always drink it with a meal.** Food slows absorption, and red wine is traditionally drunk with dinner for good reason.

**Alternate with water.** One glass of water per glass of wine slows your pace and keeps you hydrated.

**Run your own experiment.** Because different people likely react to different compounds, the most useful thing you can do is pay attention. Keep a short note of which wines you drank, how much, whether you'd eaten, and whether you got a headache. Patterns often show up within a few weeks: maybe only certain styles, regions, or price points bother you.

**Try lower-quercetin options.** If the UC Davis idea is right, wines with fewer skin compounds should be less likely to cause trouble. White wine and most rosé spend little time on grape skins, so they carry much less quercetin and fewer tannins. That fits with what many people report. Unfortunately, wine labels don't list quercetin content, and it varies even within the same grape variety, so you can't choose a "low-quercetin red" from the label alone. Researchers have noted that grapes grown with more sun exposure produce more quercetin, but that's a rough guide at best.

**Don't rely on sulfite-free wines.** As explained above, sulfites are unlikely to be the cause for most people. If they seem to help you, that's fine, but don't expect them to.

**If you have migraines, treat wine as a known trigger.** Talk to your doctor about your pattern. Some people with migraine find they can tolerate small amounts on low-stress, well-rested days and not otherwise. Others decide it's not worth it.

**Ask a doctor before trying antihistamines.** For people with suspected histamine intolerance, some take an antihistamine before drinking. Check with a pharmacist first, because sedating antihistamines plus alcohol can make you dangerously drowsy.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

We're a site about dihydromyricetin (DHM), a compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism, so it's fair to ask whether it helps here. The honest answer is that **no study has tested DHM on red wine headaches.**

What's known about DHM comes mostly from animal and lab research, with limited human data. Some animal studies suggest it may support the enzymes that clear alcohol and acetaldehyde, which is why people use it for hangovers. In theory, anything that helps clear acetaldehyde could matter if the quercetin explanation turns out to be right. But that's a chain of guesses, not evidence, and it would not override an enzyme being directly blocked. DHM also does nothing for histamine, sulfite reactions, or migraine.

If you already use DHM for hangovers, there's no reason to stop, and you might notice whether your wine nights feel different. Just don't treat it as a fix for a headache that hits after one glass. If you want to learn more, our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how people use it and what the research shows, and our [hangover prevention guide](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the strategies with the best evidence. A plain, single-ingredient option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), but cutting back on red wine and drinking it with food will do more for an immediate wine headache than any supplement.

## When to See a Doctor

Most red wine headaches are an annoyance rather than a danger. Still, see a doctor if:

- Wine reliably triggers headaches that feel like migraines, or your headaches are becoming more frequent or severe.
- You get wheezing, chest tightness, hives, or swelling of the lips, tongue, or face after wine. These suggest an allergic-type or sulfite reaction, not a simple headache.
- You flush bright red with a racing heart after small amounts of alcohol, which can be a sign of ALDH2 deficiency. That's linked to a higher risk of certain cancers with regular drinking, so it's worth knowing.
- You're taking medications that interact with alcohol, including some antidepressants, blood thinners, and the migraine drugs you might reach for.
- You find you need painkillers after drinking on a regular basis.

Get emergency care for a sudden, severe headache or one with neurological symptoms, as described at the top of this page.

## The Bottom Line

A headache that arrives within an hour or two of red wine is a real, recognized type of alcohol headache, and it's not the same as a hangover. The most promising explanation is the 2023 UC Davis finding that a converted form of quercetin, a compound from red grape skins, can block the enzyme that clears acetaldehyde. That's a lab finding that still needs testing in people. Histamine and tannins may matter for some drinkers, especially people with histamine intolerance or migraine. Sulfites are a real issue for a small group, mostly people with asthma, but they're an unlikely cause of ordinary wine headaches.

The practical steps are the same whichever theory is right: drink less red wine, drink it slowly with food and water, keep notes on which wines bother you, and stop at the first sign of a headache. If wine reliably sets off migraines, talk to your doctor about it. If you want to compare drinks more broadly, our guide to [which alcohol causes the least hangover](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol) ranks the options.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why does red wine give me a headache but white wine doesn't?**

Red wine is fermented with grape skins, so it carries far more skin compounds like quercetin and tannins, and usually more histamine, than white wine. A 2023 UC Davis lab study found that a converted form of quercetin can block the enzyme that clears acetaldehyde, a toxic by-product of alcohol, which could explain why red wine causes headaches at doses that white wine doesn't. This hasn't been confirmed in human trials yet.

**Are sulfites the cause of red wine headaches?**

Probably not for most people. White wine usually contains more sulfites than red, and dried fruit can contain far more than wine. True sulfite sensitivity is uncommon, mainly affects people with asthma, and usually causes wheezing or hives rather than headache. If you have breathing symptoms after wine, see a doctor.

**How do you get rid of a red wine headache fast?**

Stop drinking, have a glass or two of water, eat something, and rest in a quiet, dim room. If you need a pain reliever, take a single standard dose with food and follow the label. Acetaminophen is harder on the liver and ibuprofen or naproxen are harder on the stomach when combined with alcohol, so neither is risk-free. Get urgent care for a sudden, severe headache or one with confusion, weakness, or vision changes.

**How soon after drinking red wine can a headache start?**

The immediate type of alcohol headache usually starts within about three hours of drinking, and sometimes within the first 30 minutes to an hour after one or two glasses. That's different from a hangover headache, which shows up the next morning after heavier drinking.

**What is the UC Davis quercetin study about red wine headaches?**

Published in Scientific Reports in 2023 by Andrew Waterhouse, Apramita Devi, and Morris Levin, the study found in lab tests that quercetin glucuronide, the form quercetin takes after you absorb it, inhibits ALDH2, the enzyme that clears acetaldehyde. The researchers proposed this could cause red wine headaches. It was a lab study, not a human trial, so it's a promising hypothesis rather than a proven cause.

**Can histamine in red wine cause headaches?**

It may in some people, especially those with histamine intolerance who also react to aged cheese, cured meats, or other fermented foods. Alcohol is thought to slow the gut enzyme that breaks histamine down. However, a 2001 double-blind study found no clear link between wine histamine levels and reactions in people with wine intolerance, so histamine is unlikely to explain most red wine headaches.

**Is a red wine headache the same as a wine hangover?**

No. A red wine headache in the sense used here comes on during drinking or within a few hours and can follow a single glass. A wine hangover comes the next morning after heavier drinking and includes fatigue, nausea, and thirst as well as headache. Our wine hangover guide covers that next-morning problem.

**Does DHM prevent red wine headaches?**

There's no research testing DHM on red wine headaches. DHM is studied mainly for hangovers, mostly in animals, and it has no known effect on histamine, sulfite reactions, or migraine. Drinking less red wine, slowly and with food, is a more reliable approach for an immediate wine headache.
